title: 3-Read Friday #26: Coaching Feedback, Inclusive Classrooms, and Co-Constructed Feedback
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 26 is unusually thematically tight, with Barton explicitly apologizing for running two lesson-observation and coaching pieces in the same week because he could not ignore either post. His first pick, Paul Cline's "Feedback should improve the teacher, not the lesson," is framed through Barton's own established practice, the Hypothesis Model of lesson observation, with Barton using Cline's post to interrogate his own default reaction (simply discarding and reforming a hypothesis) when an observational prediction turns out wrong. His second pick, Ben Newmark's piece on inclusive classrooms, is introduced with a candid admission that Barton himself has never been sure what people mean by the term inclusive classroom, crediting Newmark with providing genuine definitional clarity. His third pick, Tom Sherrington's argument against written or emailed lesson feedback, is framed simply as too good to leave out despite topical overlap with Cline's piece, praised as great form with a powerful message. Unlike most issues, all three selections orbit the same underlying subject - how observers should give feedback and think about classrooms during coaching - making this one of the more unified editions of the series.

quotes: I am a huge fan of the Hypothesis Model when observing a lesson as a precursor to coaching. But what happens if your hypothesis is wrong?
Typically, I ditch it and try to form a new hypothesis. Here, Paul suggests an alternative approach.
I often hear people talking about “inclusive classrooms”, and I am never sure what they actually mean.
In this wonderful, thought-provoking piece, Ben outlines what an inclusive classroom could look like and, most importantly of all, how to create one.
Apologies for including a second piece on lesson observations and coaching this week, but I could not ignore either post.
Tom is in great form here with a powerful message for anyone lucky enough to observe a colleague teach and give them feedback.
